DiffDriver is a model-based approach to identifying Differential Positive
Selection across cancer patients. Our software is available at
https://github.com/szhaolab/diffdriver.

## Background Mutation Model Evaluation

- [BMR Prediction](BMR.html) — Mutation prediction: signature vs regular methods

## Simulation

Two complementary scenarios evaluate DiffDriver against benchmark methods
(linear regression, Fisher's exact test, binomial test, logistic regression,
[coselens](https://github.com/ggonzalezlopez/coselens), and the Mann-Whitney
rank-sum test).

### Power — phenotype drives selection

- [Simulation: Pipeline and Power Results](simulation-power.html) — Documents the
  simulation pipeline (mutations generated under a selection model where the
  phenotype is correlated with positive selection), then compares sensitivity
  (power) and the false discovery rate across all methods. Binary phenotype,
  200 genes (50 signal / 150 null), swept over selection strength and sample
  size.

### False positives — phenotype confounded with a mutational signature

- [Simulation: Phenotype–Signature Confounding](Simulation-BMR.html) — The
  phenotype is correlated with a mutational signature (LUAD signature 3,
  $R^2 = 0.78$) but has **zero** correlation with selection, so any detection is
  a false positive. Because the confounding signature inflates the background
  mutation rate, the count-based benchmarks (including Mann-Whitney) increasingly
  false-positive with sample size, while DiffDriver controls the false positive
  rate. coselens, when given each group's true background rate, also stays
  controlled. Single gene (ERBB3) with hotspots placed at the signature's peak
  context.
- [Simulation: Estimated Background under Signature Confounding](Simulation-BMR-estimated.html) —
  A stricter version of the above: instead of being *given* the true background
  rate, DiffDriver and coselens must *estimate* it from a simulated genome-wide
  silent (synonymous) mutation count matrix calibrated to the observed LUAD
  burden (~64 syn/sample). Both still control the false positive rate, whereas
  the count-based benchmarks rise to ~0.6.
